channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months
item.description: This article explores practical strategies for optimizing AI agent performance, focusing on metrics like time-to-first-token and throughput. It covers technical approaches to tool integration, infrastructure design, and the necessity of robust sandboxing for efficient agent development.

item.title: Celebrating SIM Cards
item.description: The author reflects on the surprisingly seamless experience of swapping a SIM card into a new iPhone. Despite expecting typical technical hurdles, the process worked perfectly, leading the author to appreciate the success of standard mobile technology.

item.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
item.description: The author reflects on the nature of political power by examining the lives of Lyndon B. Johnson and Robert Moses as chronicled by biographer Robert Caro. The piece serves as a preparation for an in-depth interview regarding the mechanisms and ethics of exercising influence.

item.title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
item.description: This article provides a brief historical timeline of Digital Equipment Corporation's (DEC) PDP computer series. It examines the evolution, technical specifications, and market positioning of various models from the PDP-1 through the VAX transition.

item.title: A New Kind of Chemistry
item.description: This article explores innovations in chemistry through insights from Marathon Fusion. It highlights new chemical processes and potential advancements in material science.

item.title: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions
item.description: This article advises against having public functions call each other to avoid unnecessary API coupling. It recommends refactoring shared logic into private helper functions to prevent public interfaces from becoming cluttered with internal implementation details.

item.title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
item.description: This post explores the author's experience using Qwen3-TTS to create unique, custom voiceovers for a dungeon crawler game project. It highlights the capabilities and limitations of Qwen3's three model variants, particularly regarding the trade-off between voice cloning quality and the ability to apply stylistic instructions.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This piece explores the recurring frustrations of developers working with specific programming languages. It highlights the ironic persistence of preventable errors within language ecosystems.

item.title: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a new benefit where high-tier ChatGPT subscription plans now receive matching API credits. This move follows a similar recent announcement from Anthropic, providing users with increased flexibility to build and deploy AI projects.

item.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
item.description: Simon Willison explores Spawn, a multiplayer gaming environment where users utilize AI agents to generate and modify the world in real-time through prompts. The platform demonstrates the advanced potential of agentic engineering by allowing players to create structures and creatures like dragons within a voxel-based game.

item.title: Quoting Ben Hylak
item.description: This post highlights a humorous observation about the tension between the push for headless, AI-agent-integrated products and the enduring value of traditional user interfaces. It touches on the evolving role of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in the AI ecosystem.

item.title: You can just ask AI to do things
item.description: This article discusses the emerging paradigm of using AI systems as proactive agents that can execute tasks rather than just providing information. It emphasizes the shift from simple querying to delegating complex workflows to AI models.

item.title: Fake it ‘til you make it (and then keep faking it)
item.description: The article explores the psychological and professional implications of the 'fake it till you make it' mindset. It argues that maintaining this behavior beyond initial success is a functional strategy for sustained growth and overcoming imposter syndrome.

item.title: We Won’t “Just Hang Out”
item.description: This article explores the future of human connection in a post-Singularity world. It challenges the assumption that social interaction will remain unchanged or simply continue as casual 'hanging out' once human intelligence is fundamentally transformed.

item.title: This Week in Source Control: 28 October 2026
item.description: This blog post introduces a new weekly roundup dedicated to news in source control systems, clients, and forges. It highlights the inaugural edition, which features technical insights into Anthropic's transition from Git to their custom 'Scion' version control system to handle massive scaling demands.

item.title: The Unbalanced Group Theorem
item.description: This post discusses the classification of finite simple groups, recognized as one of the most extensive projects in mathematical history. It highlights the recent achievement by Axiom in formalizing the proof of the Unbalanced Group Theorem, a key component of this massive collective work.

item.title: C++/WinRT overcorrection: Using make_self and immediately converting it to the projected interface
item.description: This post critiques the practice of using 'make_self' in C++/WinRT when the result is immediately cast to the projected interface. The author suggests this approach is an unnecessary complication compared to standard instantiation methods.

item.title: Why don’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority, so they can remain responsive?
item.description: This post explains why assigning high priority to system components like the taskbar and Task Manager does not necessarily improve responsiveness. It highlights that system performance is often limited by dependencies and waiting for resources rather than just CPU scheduling.

item.title: Psychometrics, vaccines, meat, Kowloon, luggage destruction
item.description: This post reviews a scholarly paper evaluating the psychometric reliability of a 'Dynomight' version of the MBTI, showing high correlation with the original test. Additionally, it touches on the regulatory hurdles and bioethical controversies surrounding yeast-based vaccine self-experimentation.

item.title: Gadget Review: SoundPEATS CC3 Pro Bluetooth Headphones ★★★★⯪
item.description: This review evaluates the SoundPEATS CC3 Pro Bluetooth headphones, focusing on their unique 'clip-on' design. The author praises the device's exceptional comfort, noting that they can be worn all day without irritation.

item.title: Pluralistic: Agents vs ecommerce (28 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the concept of 'agentic AI' in e-commerce, drawing parallels to his 2001 essay 'Metacrap' regarding the failures of the Semantic Web. He argues that the complexity of autonomous agents often clashes with the reality of proprietary web structures and conflicting incentives.

item.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
item.description: This post highlights insights from Ted Sanders on LLM performance and OpenAI's versioning strategy. It explains that while performance is multidimensional, model size remains the primary predictor of capabilities, and version numbers reflect release sequences rather than just incremental progress.

item.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
item.description: The 2026 GitHub Octoverse report highlights a massive surge in developer productivity, specifically noting that merged pull requests and commits have tripled. These record-breaking figures are attributed to the growing influence of agentic engineering and automated development tools.

item.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
item.description: The author identifies October 2026 as a major inflection point for 'vibe game development,' where advancements in AI models like Claude Opus 5.5 enable more sophisticated creation of 3D assets, music, and game design. By showcasing several successful experimental projects, the post argues that AI has evolved from producing superficial visuals to becoming a capable partner in actual game development.

item.title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
item.description: Amazon's engineering leadership emphasizes that not every task benefits from AI, and identifying these limitations is a sign of good professional judgment. Engineers are encouraged to document where AI falls short and share these findings to help improve workflows.

item.title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
item.description: The article emphasizes that mastery in the field of AI is not an overnight achievement but a result of consistent practice and sustained effort. It encourages readers to adopt a long-term mindset to navigate the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.

item.title: I'm Full-Time Open Source Developer Now
item.description: Developer Miguel Grinberg shares his transition to working full-time on his 18 open-source projects. He explains the shift from balancing development with a day job and invites the community to support his ongoing efforts.

item.title: The upvote dilemma
item.description: Herman describes his decision to hide visible upvote counts on his platform, Bear, to reduce the 'popularity contest' dynamic and encourage content discovery based on merit rather than social proof. While keeping the underlying upvote mechanism for ranking, he aims to mitigate the negative psychological effects and the pressure to optimize for metrics.

item.title: Weekly Update 527: Cybergeddon News v. Reality
item.description: This update analyzes the recent hype surrounding 'Cybergeddon' headlines, noting that the predicted massive internet outages never materialized. It highlights the difficulty in verifying technical claims, specifically regarding the PHP2Shell exploit, contrasting sensationalist news with observable reality.

item.title: MTL-style circuit simulator
item.description: The article explores using the MTL-style pattern, a form of final tagless encoding, to build a circuit simulator in Haskell. It demonstrates how to define a clear boundary of operations through a type class to improve code structure and maintainability.

item.title: Inches & Miles
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The article reflects on the history of internet startups harvesting user data through seemingly helpful features, such as Facebook's early 'Like' button. The author draws a parallel between this past era of digital exploitation and the current practices of AI startups, warning that history may be repeating itself.

item.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False
item.description: This post discusses the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) and the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which posits that no sub-exponential algorithm can solve 3-SAT. The author explores the implications of this hypothesis and recent theoretical developments regarding its validity.

item.title: Book Review: You Could Do Something Amazing with Your Life [You Are Raoul Moat] - Andrew Hankinson ★★★★☆
item.description: This blog post reviews Andrew Hankinson's book about Raoul Moat, praising its unique second-person narrative style. The reviewer highlights how the author avoids sensationalism by utilizing the subject's own words to provide a nuanced perspective on his life and actions.

item.title: Pluralistic: History is something you do (27 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that the future is not a predetermined path but a contingent space shaped by human agency. He critiques the 'inevitabilism' promoted by tech influencers and policymakers, positioning science fiction as a tool to dismantle the idea that the future is beyond our control.

item.title: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge
item.description: Simon Willison showcases a GitHub Universe conference badge that functions as a color computer capable of running NES and Game Boy Color emulators. Through collaboration, developers successfully ported classic titles like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening to the badge's hardware.

item.title: Noctua Fan Swap on a Calnex Rb/GPS Frequency Reference
item.description: Jeff Geerling documents a hardware maintenance procedure for replacing a cooling fan in a Calnex Rb/GPS frequency reference unit. The guide covers the physical disassembly process, including dealing with Loctite-secured fasteners to access the internal components.

item.title: De IT-onmacht van de Nederlandse overheid
item.description: The author critiques the Dutch government's recurring struggles with information technology and their failure to acknowledge these systemic issues. Through two specific examples, the article argues that this denial prevents meaningful reform and long-term improvement.

item.title: Why My Dad Didn’t Have a Cell Phone
item.description: This post reflects on the increasing mental burden caused by modern communication tools that demand constant attention. It highlights the author's father, who foresaw this issue decades ago by rejecting cell phones to preserve his autonomy and personal time.

item.title: Package Management Devroom at FOSDEM 2027: Call for Participation
item.description: The Package Management devroom is returning to FOSDEM 2027 and is currently seeking talk submissions until December 1st. Organizers are looking for presentations from maintainers focusing on technical challenges like dependency resolution, supply chain security, and metadata standards.

item.title: Inversion in an ellipse
item.description: This post continues a series on geometric duality, focusing on the concepts of poles and polars in the context of ellipses. It explains the historical origins of these terms, tracing them back to spherical geometry and their subsequent extension to other geometric figures.

item.title: Where else to find me
item.description: The author outlines the various platforms where readers can find their work beyond the primary blog. This includes multiple specialized X accounts categorized by field and RSS feeds for updates.

item.title: Puzzling out why a program doesn’t work when run from a batch file, but works when double-clicked from Explorer
item.description: This post explains the technical discrepancies between executing a program via a batch file versus double-clicking it in Windows Explorer. It highlights how differences in environmental contexts and execution methods can lead to unexpected program behavior.

item.title: Scattered thoughts on how doing math feels these days
item.description: The author reflects on the rapid evolution of AI in mathematics, noting a shift from skepticism to astonishment as capabilities grew exponentially in late 2025. Despite AI's ability to perform specific tasks quickly, the author reports only a 50% increase in overall productivity, arguing that current workflows are not yet optimized for AI integration.

item.title: Theatre Review: Opera UnTouched's "The Telephone" ★★★★★
item.description: This review covers Opera UnTouched's unique production of 'The Telephone,' a comic opera performed within an actual office setting. The author highlights the immersive experience and charm of the unconventional venue, ultimately giving the performance a five-star rating.

item.title: Pluralistic: Sovereign citizens, but for news (26 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the increasingly predatory practices of major media outlets, specifically targeting a troubling 'terms of service' policy at the LA Times. He highlights how news organizations are adopting aggressive, 'sovereign citizen'-style legal tactics that prioritize institutional control over user rights.

item.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
item.description: OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra, a mid-range model optimized for visual reasoning, efficient computer use, and natural writing. Simon Willison notes that it serves as a balanced alternative to existing models, offering improved speed and specific task performance for both developers and general subscribers.

item.title: Quoting Jason Koebler
item.description: Users struggling with the lack of customer support on big tech platforms are turning to ChatGPT for assistance. Consequently, the AI is mistakenly directing these users to 404 Media, incorrectly identifying their routine tech issues as journalistic scoops.

item.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
item.description: Simon Willison evaluates 'webframe', a Go-based tool that runs web pages like programs using system-native browser engines. He utilizes an AI-generated research report to assess its potential as a lightweight alternative to heavier scraping tools like Playwright.

item.title: Seam Cutter
item.description: Simon Willison introduces Seam Cutter, a web-based tool designed to crop out sections from the middle of images. It allows users to make horizontal or vertical cuts and shift the sides, providing a practical way to redact content from long, stitched screenshots.

item.title: MacOS Extensions pack for the Apple Network Server v1.0
item.description: This article explores the history and technical recovery of the Apple Network Server (ANS), a rare Unix-based server from the late 90s. The author details the discovery of prototype ROMs that allow the machine to boot Mac OS, highlighting the hardware challenges and limitations of these early experimental versions.

item.title: A rising tide raises all rents
item.description: This article explores the economic implications of the AI productivity boom, arguing that gains will largely be captured by rent-seekers and incumbents rather than the general public. The author proposes implementing mechanisms similar to a Land-Value Tax to manage scarce resources and prevent extreme wealth concentration.

item.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
item.description: This article examines the economic factors driving drastic price reductions in Large Language Model (LLM) APIs by leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic. It explores the industry shift from profit-maximizing pricing to aggressive market capture and efficiency-based cost structures.

item.title: Poles and polars
item.description: This article explores the geometric concepts of poles and polars on a sphere, explaining their definitions and theoretical origins. It builds on previous discussions regarding polar triangles and their application in geometry.

item.title: Computing polar triangles with linear algebra
item.description: This article explains how to use linear algebra to construct polar triangles on a sphere. It builds upon previous concepts to provide a rigorous mathematical framework for the existence and construction of these triangles.

item.title: Duality in spherical trigonometry
item.description: This article explores the concept of duality in spherical trigonometry, specifically focusing on the relationship between the law of cosines for sides and the law of cosines for angles. It explains how these two formulas are mathematically symmetric and can be interchanged to solve spherical geometry problems.

item.title: Gadget Review: LiberNovo Omni - the USB-C powered office chair ★★★★⯪
item.description: The LiberNovo Omni is an office chair that features USB-C recharging capabilities, marking a unique trend in office furniture. The review highlights its exceptional comfort, including full foam cushions and an ergonomic recline, alongside its innovative power integration.

item.title: Don't anthropomorphize big tech companies
item.description: This article argues against the tendency to attribute human personality traits or intentions to large technology corporations. It suggests that viewing these companies as profit-driven entities rather than conscious actors provides a more accurate understanding of their behavior.

item.title: Interesting systemd features you may not know about
item.description: This article highlights several lesser-known systemd features that are particularly useful for managing transient tasks. Key capabilities include memory limits, execution time constraints, and path-based triggers, which provide robust control for ephemeral workloads.

item.title: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
item.description: Steve Blank analyzes the geopolitical fallout following the U.S. decision to restrict Starlink access in Ukraine. He argues this event serves as a wake-up call for European policymakers, prompting a push for technological sovereignty and alternatives to American-controlled infrastructure.

item.title: Reading List 10/24/26
item.description: This post provides a curated list of interesting readings covering a diverse range of topics, including urban planning policy, aerospace industry developments, financial market short-selling, and artificial intelligence advancements. It serves as a digest for readers interested in construction, technology, and economic trends.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 24 October 2026
item.description: This week's digest covers the widespread security implications of compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs, which necessitated emergency updates across numerous package managers and language runtimes. The post provides a comprehensive list of patched versions for tools including uv, pip, conda, and various language environments like Python, Java, and Node.js.

item.title: List of Vim forks
item.description: This post provides a curated list of notable Vim forks, including Neovim, Vim Classic, EVi, and MacVim. It clarifies the scope by excluding Vim-inspired editors, plugins, and distributions.

item.title: Book Review: Get Ahead of Being Dead by Evie King ★★★★☆
item.description: This blog post reviews Evie King's book 'Get Ahead of Being Dead', which explores the bureaucratic and administrative complexities of death. The author highlights how the book provides insight into the overwhelming post-mortem logistics, such as settling bills and managing family disputes.

item.title: battledrones v14: Compass Rose, a four player map
item.description: Simon Willison has updated his 'Battledrones' game to version 14, introducing a new four-player map called 'Compass Rose.' The update leverages AI-generated code from Claude Opus 5.5 to implement multi-player support via WebSockets and adds new robot color designs.

item.title: An Ion Storm!, Part 2: The Return to Ground Level
item.description: This article chronicles a pivotal moment in the history of game developer Ion Storm, focusing on John Romero's turbulent career and the rumors surrounding his departure. It contextualizes the rise and fall of the studio within the broader narrative of 1990s gaming industry culture.

item.title: One Small Bug
item.description: This post illustrates a conversation between a developer and an AI agent, showing how the AI fixes bugs while simultaneously discovering and remediating complex security vulnerabilities in the project's infrastructure. It highlights the hidden risks in automated toolchains, dependency management, and CI/CD configurations.

item.title: Why didn’t we use the COM static store to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
item.description: This post explains why the COM static store was not used to manage the cleanup of unmarshalable delegates. It concludes that the mechanism failed because it performed cleanup operations at the incorrect time.

item.title: Why didn’t we use Co­Register­Initialize­Spy to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
item.description: This post explores the technical constraints and reasoning behind why a specific COM API, CoRegisterInitializeSpy, was not suitable for cleaning up unmarshalable delegates. It highlights the complexities of system architecture and developer decision-making in legacy software.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This post discusses the inherent frustrations of language-specific design flaws that lead to recurring, avoidable errors. It highlights the irony of developers accepting broken tools as a standard part of their workflow.

item.title: More phishing messages via Booking.com and Novotel
item.description: The author shares a personal experience of receiving targeted phishing messages shortly after booking a hotel through Booking.com. The post analyzes the indicators of these fraudulent messages, highlighting how attackers exploit stolen booking data to impersonate service providers.

item.title: Pluralistic: Critique and writing (23 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow discusses the transformative impact of peer-based writing workshops on a writer's development. He highlights how these groups provide essential external motivation, discipline, and validation for emerging writers.

item.title: Quick Study
item.description: Quick Study is a web-based tool that uses the Sobel edge detection algorithm to transform photographs into simulated paintings using the HTML canvas element. Developed via Claude prompts, the project demonstrates how LLMs can generate functional visual art tools without external libraries.

item.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
item.description: Moonshot has introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro, a high-performance AI model that offers competitive performance benchmarks against industry leaders like GPT-6 and Claude Opus. The article highlights the model's pricing structure, upcoming open-weight release, and demonstrates how to interface with it using the LLM CLI tool.

item.title: Ubiquiti's $99 Vape Detector is actually pretty good
item.description: The author explores air quality monitoring, specifically investigating a $99 Ubiquiti vape detector as a potential tool for tracking CO2 and other pollutants. This review is part of a broader series examining various air quality sensors for home and studio use.

item.title: If people would just
item.description: The article argues that relying on people to 'just' behave is a flawed approach to system design. Instead of wishing for perfect compliance, designers should build systems that physically or structurally prevent errors and misconduct by acknowledging the reality of human behavior.

item.title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
item.description: This article explores the future trajectory of semiconductor manufacturing through insights gained from a tour of Intel's most advanced fabrication facility. It combines leadership perspectives and firsthand observations to project the evolution of chip technology by 2045.

item.title: NYC, New Webinar, Differential Testing
item.description: The author shares personal updates and introduces the concept of nondeterministic differential testing. The post explains how to verify consistency when translating programs between languages, highlighting the challenges introduced by nondeterminism compared to standard deterministic testing.

item.title: Script dependencies with Nix
item.description: This article demonstrates how to use the Nix package manager to handle script dependencies on non-NixOS Linux distributions. By encapsulating Python and system dependencies like aplay within a Nix shell, users can ensure their scripts remain reliable and reproducible.

item.title: Working around a strange Python problem
item.description: The author encounters a mysterious Python error following a system-wide update. The issue is traced to multiple PEP 723 metadata blocks, highlighting the complexities of managing script dependencies and metadata standards.

item.title: How the eMudrha certificate debacle might have happened
item.description: This post examines the security failure at eMudrha, where extremely weak, predictable numbers were used as secret keys for certificates. It highlights the dangers of inadequate entropy in cryptographic systems and explains why such simple values are fundamentally insecure.

item.title: The number of points on an elliptic curve
item.description: This article explains the mathematical definition of elliptic curves over finite fields, which are foundational to modern cryptography. It discusses how points on these curves are determined by the equation y² = x³ + ax + b and mentions the distribution of these points.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This piece uses satire to comment on the repetitive nature of technical failures and security vulnerabilities in specific programming languages. It highlights the recurring frustration of developers who consistently encounter the same systemic issues.

item.title: Gadget Review: Mokin 17 Port USB-C Tower ★★☆☆☆
item.description: This review evaluates the Mokin 17-port USB-C tower, a feature-heavy docking station. The author highlights the device's extensive connectivity options while expressing confusion over the inclusion of unnecessary features like an LCD weather display.

item.title: Pluralistic: Adversarial interoperability is a team sport (21 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that digital enshittification can be countered through adversarial interoperability, leveraging the universal nature of Turing-complete machines to restore user control. He emphasizes that restoring features or blocking unwanted changes is a collaborative effort that requires collective action rather than individual "jailbreaks."

item.title: Productivity
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The article explores the productivity paradox where automation and AI agents, instead of saving time, often lead to increased workloads and constant busyness. It highlights how the expectation to produce more results perpetually consumes any time saved by new technologies.

item.title: DE STAAT - FREEDOM (Official Music Video)
item.description: Simon Willison shares a music video by the Dutch band De Staat that features a notable visual effects sequence. The post highlights the use of generative AI in creating a surreal clip of a pelican riding a bicycle.

item.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.description: Anthropic has donated its Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation, to ensure open and vendor-neutral development. Simon Willison highlights this move, noting that he previously predicted this transition and demonstrating how he used MCP to verify his past commentary.

item.title: Quoting Armin Ronacher
item.description: This post features a quote from Armin Ronacher regarding the current state of software development. It suggests that the proliferation of poor software practices over the past three decades has left the industry vulnerable to the challenges posed by AI.

item.title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
item.description: The article argues that software performance issues are primarily rooted in poor architectural design rather than the choice of programming language. It suggests that developer productivity and algorithmic efficiency are more significant factors in system speed than low-level execution speed.

item.title: Rails is a JIT compiler
item.description: The article explores optimizing Ruby on Rails enum method generation by replacing dynamic method dispatching with static code generation. The author identifies that using public_send and define_method with blocks creates unnecessary runtime overhead, proposing module_eval as a more efficient alternative.

item.title: Objects, attributes, maps, oh my!
item.description: This article explores how dynamically typed languages often use hash tables to store object attributes, providing code examples in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript. It explains that while this approach is flexible, it introduces performance overhead due to high memory latency and inefficient property lookups compared to in-line storage.

item.title: Going Somewhere
item.description: The author reflects on a meaningful conversation held during a drive home from O'Hare airport. The piece highlights a single impactful concluding remark made by the driver, Vicky.

item.title: No Need for Retirement When Utopia Is Around the Corner
item.description: The author draws parallels between the Cold War-era nuclear strategy environment at RAND Corporation and the current rhetoric surrounding modern AI development. By reflecting on Daniel Ellsberg's experiences, the post highlights how both groups share a sense of moral burden, perceived 'insider' knowledge, and a belief that their work is essential to saving the world.

item.title: Trust Stores Are Dependencies Too
item.description: The article highlights the risks of hardcoded certificate authority trust stores within software dependencies, using the recent eMudhra incident as a case study. It details how widespread vendor-embedded certificates prevent centralized security updates, requiring manual patching across environments and runtimes.

item.title: Backdoors, Incompetence, and Elliptic Curves
item.description: This article discusses the ongoing controversies surrounding NIST elliptic curves, specifically addressing concerns about potential backdoors and recent security failures involving broken certificates. The author reflects on the tension between security skepticism and implementation incompetence in cryptographic standards.

item.title: Deliberate imperfection
item.description: This article explores the concept of 'deliberate imperfection,' reflecting on the cyclical nature of life as described in the Book of Ecclesiastes. It suggests that embracing flaws is essential to finding harmony and meaning within the varying seasons of human experience.

item.title: Why didn’t we use Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
item.description: This post discusses why a specific Windows API function, RoRegisterForApartmentShutdown, was unsuitable for cleaning up unmarshalable delegates. It highlights the complex circular requirements that made this approach ineffective for the intended task.

item.title: Microspeak: Drain the slide, back-up slides
item.description: This post explains the corporate jargon 'drain the slide' and the usage of 'back-up slides' in PowerPoint presentations. It defines these terms within the context of professional business communication.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This piece critiques the recurring, preventable technical issues inherent in specific programming languages. It highlights the irony of users accepting persistent failure as a standard characteristic of their chosen development environment.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This post critiques the persistent design flaws and recurring security vulnerabilities inherent in specific programming languages. It highlights the irony of developers accepting these avoidable errors as inevitable parts of their environment.
